# Integrating LLM-Based Agents into Resource Allocation in Data-Driven Business Process Simulation

This repository contains the public research artifact for experiments on
LLM-based resource allocation in data-driven business process simulation.
The repository is intended to support inspection and reproducibility of
the implemented experiments. It contains data, source code, and result
files only; draft writing materials are intentionally not included.

## Purpose

The experiments test whether an LLM can replace the resource-allocation rule
without taking control of the remaining simulation model. The centralized
condition selects one resource from the activity-specific set presented by the
simulator; observed handover patterns may narrow this set. The AgentSimulator
integration collects independent bids from shortlisted resource agents. Both
conditions retain simulator control of process execution, timing, checks that a
resource can perform an activity, availability, final allocation, and event-log
generation.

## Repository Contents

```text
data/       Prepared public benchmark data and license information
src/        Python scripts for data preparation, simulation, and evaluation
results/    Archived result summaries used for analysis
```

The top-level files are:

- `README.md`: public repository guide.
- `ARTIFACT_MANIFEST.md`: map from the final study to archived result files.
- `CITATION.cff`: citation metadata for the research artifact.
- `requirements.txt`: minimal Python package requirements.
- `.gitignore`: local output, cache, and excluded writing folders.

## Reported Simulation Conditions

The reported LoanApp experiments compare:

- centralized LLM allocation with uniform allocation, frequency-weighted
  allocation, and a deterministic development proxy; and
- LLM resource-agent bids inside AgentSimulator with a simplified
  fixed-formula bidding rule developed for this study, using the same shortlist
  and task-allocation procedure.

The implementation also contains earlier development conditions:

The earlier lightweight simulator compares three policies:

- `central_baseline`: samples one of the resources
  that historically performed the activity.
- `agent_profile`: samples resources using learned
  activity-resource frequencies.
- `llm_agent_proxy`: uses handover priors, activity-resource priors, and
  a resource overuse penalty to emulate a constrained LLM-style local
  decision module.

The code also includes an optional `llm_agent_real` condition behind the
same constrained resource-allocation interface. The real-LLM runner supports Groq, Gemini,
OpenRouter, and custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints. It records API
successes, invalid outputs, fallbacks, latency, and token use. A missing
API key causes the experiment to stop so that fallback-only output cannot
be reported as a real-LLM result.

The optional `resource_agent_orchestrated` and
`resource_agent_autonomous` modes are diagnostic prototypes informed by
AgentSimulator's resource-agent abstraction. They add persistent resource
availability, empirical calendars, capabilities, processing-time samples,
and handover-conditioned allocation. They are not the upstream
AgentSimulator implementation and must not be reported as such. The archived
official comparison was produced by running the upstream repository and then
normalising its output with `src/import_agentsimulator_outputs.py`.

The `multi_llm_agent` condition is an integration with the upstream
AgentSimulator execution environment. For each task, AgentSimulator identifies
resource agents that can perform it. The adapter restricts the shortlist to
currently available agents when any are free; otherwise, all resources that can
perform the task remain under consideration. Each shortlisted agent receives
its own log-derived profile, current state, and bounded local memory, and
independently returns a structured bid. The integration ranks the bids and
passes the reordered candidate list to AgentSimulator's task-allocation
procedure. Upstream process discovery, calendars, durations, queues, and
resource state remain unchanged.

## Data Sources

The supporting AcademicCredentials evaluation uses the public artifact
associated with:

Chapela-Campa, D., Benchekroun, I., Baron, O., Dumas, M., Krass, D., and
Senderovich, A. 2025. "A Framework for Measuring the Quality of Business
Process Simulation Models," Information Systems 127, 102447.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.is.2024.102447

Raw AcademicCredentials logs and the original `ComputeLogDistance.py`
script are not redistributed in this repository. They should be
downloaded from the authors' public artifact and passed to the scripts
through command-line arguments.

The repository includes a prepared robustness dataset derived from:

Kirchdorfer, L., Blümel, R., Kampik, T., van der Aa, H., and
Stuckenschmidt, H. 2024. "AgentSimulator: An Agent-Based Approach for
Data-Driven Business Process Simulation," ICPM 2024.
https://doi.org/10.1109/ICPM63005.2024.10680660

The included LoanApp source log is from the public AgentSimulator GitHub
repository and is distributed there under the MIT License. The license
text is included in `data/agentsimulator_loanapp/AGENTSIMULATOR_LICENSE`.

## Reproduce the final experiments

Install the Python dependencies and run the tests:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

The API-backed experiments use Groq
`llama-3.1-8b-instant` with temperature zero. Store the API key only in
the environment:

```bash
export GROQ_API_KEY="..."
```

One centralized 100-case run:

```bash
python src/run_repeated.py \
  --train-log data/agentsimulator_loanapp/prepared/LoanApp_train.csv.gz \
  --test-log data/agentsimulator_loanapp/prepared/LoanApp_test.csv.gz \
  --output-dir outputs/centralized_seed_8200 \
  --runs 1 \
  --seed 8200 \
  --max-cases 100 \
  --include-real-llm \
  --llm-provider groq \
  --llm-model llama-3.1-8b-instant \
  --llm-min-interval 4.8 \
  --save-logs
```

One ten-case AgentSimulator run requires a clone of AgentSimulator at commit
`665a6926878859072769aa25c12fe9d6056ad510` with
`patches/agentsimulator_multi_llm_policy.patch` applied:

```bash
python src/run_agentsimulator_policy_experiment.py \
  --agentsimulator-path path/to/AgentSimulator \
  --log-path path/to/AgentSimulator/raw_data/LoanApp.csv.gz \
  --output-dir outputs/agentsimulator_seed_9400 \
  --policy multi_llm_agent \
  --max-cases 10 \
  --top-k 2 \
  --memory-size 3 \
  --seed 9400 \
  --llm-provider groq \
  --llm-model llama-3.1-8b-instant \
  --llm-min-interval 4.8
```

The fixed-formula comparison uses the internal policy name
`mock_multi_agent`. The same runner accepts `--scenario high_load` and
`--scenario resource_unavailability`. See `src/README.md` for the remaining
commands and `ARTIFACT_MANIFEST.md` for the archived outputs.

API responses are cached in `llm_response_cache.jsonl`. The cache stores model
outputs and call diagnostics, not the API key.

## Reported results

The centralized experiment contains three paired 100-case runs with seeds
8200, 8300, and 8400. All 2,192 LLM responses selected resources that could
perform the activity; no rule-based replacement was used. Compared with
frequency-weighted allocation, the LLM reduced mean Circadian Workforce
Distribution distance from 9.511 to 8.788, but increased resource-frequency
distance from 0.072 to 0.583 and used only 10--11 of 19 resources.

The AgentSimulator experiment contains three paired ten-case runs with seeds
9400, 9500, and 9600. All 445 LLM bids followed the required response format;
no replacement was used. LLM bidding had lower mean activity-frequency
distance, resource-frequency distance, and cycle-time relative error than the
fixed-formula comparison, but higher trace-variant distance. Cycle-time error
varied from 2.39% to 102.73% across the three LLM runs.

The what-if runs increase the case-arrival rate by dividing inter-arrival
intervals by 1.6 or make two resources unavailable. Allocation rules produced
different responses in cycle time, completed-case rate, work in process, and
resource utilization. No observed outcome is available for either change, so
the results measure sensitivity rather than scenario accuracy.

The same seed aligns the initial random-number setting, but a changed
allocation can alter later resource state and cause subsequent trajectories to
diverge. The paired results are descriptive. They do not isolate the effect of
the LLM, and the study does not show consistent improvement across established
BPS quality measures.

Earlier proxy, dataset-screening, and single-seed pilot results remain under
`results/` as development records. They are not part of the final comparison.
